Your RRSP refund, every payday: reducing tax at source instead of waiting for spring

If you contribute to an RRSP from each paycheque, the tax saving usually comes back months later as a refund. Compare that with having less tax withheld each payday so the saving is invested at once, and see why spending the refund matters even more.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 27 October 2026 · 7 min read
Sources reviewed 27 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Every path costs you the same $500 a month after tax. Reducing tax at source lets $696 go in each month, about $8,357 a year; the spring-refund path puts in $500 a month and invests each refund in May of the following year. The 28.2% rate is the tax one more dollar of deduction saves; a large deduction can cross into a lower bracket. The return of 6% is smooth and hypothetical, fees are inside it, and RRSP room is assumed to cover every contribution. RRSP balances are compared before the tax due on later withdrawals, which applies to every path in the same way.

The central idea

An RRSP contribution saves tax at your marginal rate, but with ordinary payroll withholding that saving reaches you only as a refund after you file. Contributing through payroll, or getting a CRA letter of authority with Form T1213, moves the saving into each pay so the same monthly effort buys a larger contribution straight away. The timing gain is modest; the much bigger risk is that the spring refund is spent rather than invested.

01

Where the RRSP tax saving goes while you wait

Many people invest in an RRSP a little at a time: a fixed amount from each paycheque into a balanced fund or an index fund. That is dollar-cost averaging from earnings, and it works the same way inside an RRSP as anywhere else. What is different is the tax. Each dollar contributed can be deducted from income, which saves tax at your marginal rate. Under ordinary payroll withholding, though, your employer keeps deducting tax as if you had made no contribution. The saving builds up with CRA during the year and comes back as a refund after you file the following spring.

So a monthly saver is, in effect, making a once-a-year lump-sum investment of the tax saving, roughly a year late. This guide asks what that delay costs, how the rules let you remove it, and what happens to the plan if the refund never makes it back into the RRSP.

02

How much a deduction saves depends on your bracket

The first chart shows the 2026 statutory rates CRA lists for federal tax and for British Columbia, combined band by band. The federal rate starts at 14% on taxable income up to CAD 58,523 and rises to 33% above CAD 258,482; BC’s rates run from 5.6% to 20.5%. Combined, they run from 19.6% in the lowest band to 53.5% in the highest. An RRSP deduction comes off the top of your taxable income, so it saves the rate of the band you are in. For taxable income between CAD 58,523 and CAD 100,728 in BC, that is 28.2%, the default in the calculator.

Two cautions. These are bracket rates before the basic personal amount and other credits; at low incomes the credits can mean the deduction saves less than the chart shows. And a large deduction can cross into a lower band, so the last dollars save a lower rate. The marginal and average tax guide shows the slices. RRSP room limits the deduction too: 18% of the previous year’s earned income, up to CRA’s dollar limit of CAD 33,810 for 2026 and CAD 35,390 for 2027, plus any unused room.

03

Three ways to save the same monthly amount

The calculator holds your monthly effort fixed: the default is CAD 500 a month after tax. It then follows three routes for 25 years with a hypothetical 6% fund return:

  1. Tax reduced at source. Less tax is withheld from each pay, so the same CAD 500 of take-home pay funds a contribution of CAD 500 ÷ (1 − 28.2%) = about CAD 696 a month, about CAD 8,357 a year. There is no RRSP refund, because the saving was already received.
  2. Spring refund invested. CAD 500 a month goes in, and each refund is invested in May of the following year. The first refund is 28.2% of CAD 6,000, or CAD 1,692. Each refund is also an RRSP contribution, so it produces a smaller refund of its own the year after.
  3. Refund spent. CAD 500 a month goes in, and the refunds go to other spending.

The second chart shows the first two years. By the end of year 1 the reduced-at-source RRSP holds about CAD 8,626 against CAD 6,193 in the other two; the spring-refund route closes part of the gap in May of year 2 and keeps chasing it. The third chart shows the long run. After 25 years the reduced-at-source route is worth about CAD 473,246 and the spring-refund route about CAD 463,970, a gap of about CAD 9,276. The refund-spent route ends near CAD 339,790, about CAD 124,000 behind the spring-refund route.

To keep the comparison fair, the spring-refund value at each year-end counts the refund still owed for that year, plus the refunds it would generate in turn. With a 0% return the first two routes then end exactly level: the difference is only timing.

04

When the timing gap is worth acting on

The heatmap repeats the comparison for marginal rates of 20% to 50% and fund returns of 0% to 9%. The gap grows with both: a higher rate means a larger refund waiting with CRA, and a higher return means the months of waiting cost more. At a 20% rate and a 3% return it is about CAD 1,781 over 25 years; at a 50% rate and a 9% return it is about CAD 75,275. A higher expected return also comes with more risk: the money moved forward is invested sooner, so in a year when the fund falls early it can buy at higher prices than the refund later would. Over many years, though, investing earnings as they arrive is the same logic the TFSA payday guide applies to paycheque money: there is no lump sum to stage, so waiting has no expected-return benefit.

The larger lesson is the refund-spent line. A refund feels like a windfall, but in this plan it is part of the contribution. A refund used for spending turns a pre-tax RRSP contribution of about CAD 696 a month into an after-tax one of CAD 500, which the RRSP-versus-TFSA comparison in the account guide shows is the step that removes most of an RRSP’s advantage.

05

How to have less tax withheld

  • Group RRSP or payroll contributions. CRA’s payroll guidance says that an RRSP contribution an employer withholds from pay and makes on the employee’s behalf automatically reduces the pay on which tax is deducted. No form is needed; the saving appears on each pay stub.
  • Your own RRSP at a bank, dealer or fund company. Your employer needs a letter of authority from CRA before it can deduct less tax. You ask for it with Form T1213, Request to Reduce Tax Deductions at Source, with documents showing the contributions you will make, such as a pre-authorized contribution schedule. CRA usually issues the letter for one tax year and generally will not issue one if you have a balance owing or unfiled returns, so it has to be renewed each year. Quebec residents also deal with Revenu Québec for provincial tax.
  • Keep the promise. The reduced withholding assumes the contributions are made. If they stop, you will owe the tax when you file. Keep the pre-authorized contributions running even in a bad market; the crash contribution guide shows what pausing does.
  • Leave room for the timing of the request. A request filed late in the year leaves fewer pays to spread the reduction over. CRA aims to issue refunds for online returns within about two weeks, so the refund route’s delay comes mostly from waiting for the year to end and the filing season, not from processing.

06

What this does not change

Reducing tax at source changes when the tax saving arrives, not its size. The deduction is still limited by RRSP room, and over-contributing more than CAD 2,000 above your limit is taxed at 1% a month. RRSP withdrawals are taxable income later, so the comparison is between RRSP balances before that tax, which applies to every route in the same way; the RRSP withdrawal guide covers it. If you expect a much lower income soon, for example a parental leave or a year of study, the deduction timing guide tests whether to contribute now and deduct later, in which case reducing withholding this year would be the wrong step.

Finally, the fund inside the RRSP is unchanged. A balanced fund in an RRSP can still fall in value; the account defers tax, and the payroll route only changes how fast money reaches the fund.
